templates.stem: {^driver} drives {~vehicle} at a steady {speed} miles per hour for {hours} hours. How far does the {vehicle} travel?

distractors.error: added the rate to the time instead of multiplying them
dropped an hour of travel time
counted one hour too many
halved the distance for no reason in the problem

solution_steps: The rate is {speed} miles per hour and the time is {hours} hours.
templates.recognition_cue: Two of {{distance, rate, time}} are given and the third is missing. Write d = rt and fill in what you have.

templates.stem: {driver} travels {route} for {dist} miles at an average speed of {speed} miles per hour. How long does the trip take?

distractors.error: rounded the division up instead of working it out
rounded the division down instead of working it out
divided by half the speed, doubling the time
added time that the problem never mentions

solution_steps: Rearrange d = rt into t = d / r.
The distance is {dist} miles and the rate is {speed} miles per hour.
templates.recognition_cue: When the question asks 'how long', you want t = d / r. Divide the distance by the speed, never the other way round.

templates.stem: A {item} at {shop} is marked {price} dollars. It is on sale at {pct} percent off. What is the sale price?

distractors.error: gave the size of the discount instead of the price you pay
added the discount to the price instead of subtracting it
subtracted the percent as if it were a dollar amount
took only half the discount

templates.recognition_cue: 'Percent off' asks for what you pay, not what you save. Find the discount, then subtract it, or multiply by (100 - percent).

templates.stem: The {thing} paid by {who} rose from {=original|money} to {=final|money}. By what percent did it increase?

distractors.error: divided the change by the new amount instead of the original
gave the dollar increase rather than the percent increase
estimated rather than dividing the change by the original
doubled the correct percent

solution_steps: Percent change divides the change by the ORIGINAL amount: {=final-original|money} / {=original|money}.
templates.recognition_cue: Percent change always divides by where you started, not where you ended up. Change over original.

templates.stem: {^pair} split {total} {thing} in the ratio {small} to {big}. How many {thing} did {bigname} get?

distractors.error: gave the smaller share instead of the larger one
split the total evenly, ignoring the ratio
used one share too many when dividing up the total
dropped a share while working out the remainder

solution_steps: The ratio {small} to {big} means {=small+big} equal parts in total.
templates.recognition_cue: Add the ratio numbers to get the number of parts, divide the total by that to size one part, then multiply by the share you were asked for.

templates.stem: {^n1} {item} at {place} cost {=cost1|money}. At the same price per {item}, what do {n2} {item} cost?

distractors.error: added one extra unit's price to the total
added the quantity to the price instead of scaling
halved the answer
priced only the additional units, not the whole order

templates.recognition_cue: Same price per unit means a proportion. Find the unit price first, then multiply by the new quantity.

templates.stem: {who} borrows {=principal|money} {purpose} at {rate} percent simple interest per year for {years} years. What is the total amount owed at the end?

distractors.error: gave only the interest, not the total owed
charged interest for one year instead of {years}
slipped a decimal place converting the percent
treated the percent as a flat dollar charge

solution_steps: Simple interest is I = P x r x t, with r written as a decimal.
templates.recognition_cue: Simple interest never compounds. Work out I = Prt, then read the question again to see whether it wants the interest alone or the total.

templates.stem: {who} of {=principal|money} {verb} {=interest|money} in simple interest over {years} years. What was the annual interest rate?

distractors.error: forgot to divide by the number of years
gave the total rate over the whole period, not the annual rate
rounded the division instead of computing it
doubled the correct rate

solution_steps: Start from I = P x r x t and solve for r: r = I / (P x t).
As a percent that is {=interest*100/(principal*years)|percent} per year.
templates.recognition_cue: If the interest and the time are both given, divide the interest by principal x years. Skipping the years is the classic slip.

templates.stem: {a} produces {rateA} {thing} per hour and {b} produces {rateB} per hour. Running together, how long do they take to produce {total} {thing}?

distractors.error: used only the faster machine's rate
used only the slower machine's rate
added time the problem does not call for
doubled the time, as if the machines ran one after the other

solution_steps: Working together, the rates add: {rateA} + {rateB} = {=rateA+rateB} {thing} per hour.
templates.recognition_cue: When two things work at the same time, add their rates before dividing. Rates add; times do not.

templates.stem: {a} completes {rateA} {thing} per hour and {b} completes {rateB} per hour. They work side by side for {hours} hours and finish {total} {thing} between them. How many did {a} complete?

distractors.error: gave the other worker's share
split the work evenly, ignoring the different rates
counted an extra hour for this worker
added the rate to the time instead of multiplying

solution_steps: {^a} works at {rateA} {thing} per hour for {hours} hours.
templates.recognition_cue: If the question names one worker, use that worker's own rate and time. The combined total is only there to tempt you into splitting it.

templates.stem: {^who} records {thing}. The first four are {s1}, {s2}, {s3} and {s4}. If the average of all five is exactly {avg}, what is the fifth value?

distractors.error: assumed the missing value equals the average
multiplied the average by four instead of five
arithmetic slip when subtracting the known total
averaged only the four known values

solution_steps: An average of {avg} across 5 values means the total is {avg} x 5 = {=avg*5}.
The four known values add to {s1} + {s2} + {s3} + {s4} = {=known}.
templates.recognition_cue: Turn the average back into a total first: total = average x count. Then subtract what you already know.

templates.stem: Over four days, {who} recorded {a}, {b}, {c} and {d} {thing}. What was the average per day?

distractors.error: gave the four-day total rather than the daily average
divided by three days instead of four
averaged only the highest and lowest days
arithmetic slip in the division

solution_steps: Divide by the number of days, 4.
templates.recognition_cue: Average = sum divided by how many. Count the values carefully; dividing by the wrong count is the usual error.

templates.stem: {^who} measures {thing} at {yards} yards and {extrafeet} feet. How many inches is that in total? (1 yard = 3 feet, 1 foot = 12 inches.)

distractors.error: stopped at feet and never converted to inches
treated the yards as if they were already feet
converted yards straight to inches at 12 per yard
multiplied by 36 twice

templates.recognition_cue: Convert one step at a time and write the unit after every number. Yards to feet to inches, never yards straight to inches.

templates.stem: Each of {boxes} {thing} at {place} weighs {pounds} pounds. What is the combined weight in ounces? (1 pound = 16 ounces.)

distractors.error: gave the weight in pounds and never converted
converted one box only, ignoring the count
used 12 ounces per pound instead of 16
added one extra pound's worth of ounces

solution_steps: Total weight in pounds: {pounds} x {boxes} = {=pounds*boxes} pounds.
There are 16 ounces in a pound.
templates.recognition_cue: Do the counting first, then the one conversion at the end. Converting early means converting several times and inviting a slip.

templates.stem: {^container} holds {good} {goodname} and {other} {othername}. If one item is drawn at random, what is the probability that it is one of the {goodname}?

distractors.error: found the probability of the other outcome
divided by the other group instead of the total
assumed two outcomes means an even chance
halved a correct probability

templates.recognition_cue: The denominator is always the total number of items, not the number of the other kind. Add the groups first.

templates.stem: {^container} contains {total} items, of which {target} are {targetname}. What is the probability that a single item drawn at random is NOT one of the {targetname}?

distractors.error: gave the chance of drawing the named item rather than not drawing it
divided by the named group instead of the total
assumed a two-way split means an even chance
subtracted the count from 100 instead of the percent

solution_steps: The chance of drawing one of the {targetname} is {target} / {total} = {=target*100/total|percent}.
'Not' means the complement: subtract from 100 percent.
templates.recognition_cue: The word NOT signals the complement. Work out the straightforward probability, then subtract it from 100 percent.

templates.stem: {who} buys {item} for {=cost|money} each and sells them for {=price|money} each. If {units} are sold, what is the total profit?

distractors.error: gave total revenue and never subtracted the cost
gave the profit on a single item, not on all {units}
added the cost instead of subtracting it
gave what the goods cost rather than the profit

solution_steps: Multiply by the number sold: {units} x {=price-cost|money}.
templates.recognition_cue: Profit is always selling price minus cost. Work out profit per unit first, then scale up; revenue on its own is the trap.

templates.stem: {^who} pays {=cost|money} for {item} and marks it up {markup} percent of cost. What is the selling price?

distractors.error: gave the markup amount rather than the selling price
subtracted the markup as if it were a discount
added the percent as a flat dollar figure
applied only half the markup

solution_steps: The markup is {markup} percent of the {=cost|money} cost.
templates.recognition_cue: Markup is figured on cost, discount on list price. Read which one the question names before you multiply.
